summary: Describes rig, a tool that queries the LISP-DDT hierarchy, similar in spirit to dig.

plainLanguage.summary: A probe to ask the LISP phone-book helpers for details.

subtitle: A diagnostic tool for querying the LISP delegated database hierarchy.

tldr.problem: When using LISP's delegated database tree (DDT) to manage address mappings in networks, operators need a way to manually query and troubleshoot the mapping database hierarchy.
tldr.mechanism: The 'rig' tool allows network administrators to send encapsulated Map-Request messages to DDT nodes and follow referrals through the hierarchy, displaying information about which node handles which address prefixes.
tldr.outcome: Rig provides essential diagnostic capabilities for LISP-DDT networks, similar to DNS diagnostics tools, enabling operators to verify correct configuration and troubleshoot mapping issues.

today: RFC 8112 is an Informational RFC published in May 2017. The rig tool is documented as an informational reference for implementing diagnostic capabilities in LISP-DDT systems. It remains a standard diagnostic tool for operators deploying LISP-based networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RIG stands for Referral Internet Groper, a diagnostic tool for the Locator/ID Separation Protocol Delegated Database Tree (LISP-DDT). LISP separates IP addresses into two namespaces: Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) used within sites and Routing Locators (RLOCs) used on the transit Internet. LISP-DDT is a hierarchical distributed database that maps EIDs to RLOCs using a tree of delegated nodes.

The rig tool allows network devices and administrators to manually query this LISP-DDT hierarchy. It can be run on ITRs (Ingress Tunnel Routers), ETRs (Egress Tunnel Routers), Map-Resolvers, Map-Servers, DDT nodes, or even host systems. It works similarly to the 'lig' tool for general LISP mapping lookups, but specifically traces DDT delegation.
sections.plainLanguage: Rig is a tool for asking the LISP phone-book system questions like 'who handles this address?' and following the chain of answers to see the whole structure.

sections.title: How RIG Works
sections.content:
RIG queries the LISP-DDT hierarchy by sending an Encapsulated Control Message (ECM) Map-Request to a DDT node. When the DDT node receives the request for a particular EID, it responds with a Map-Referral message containing either (1) a referral to other DDT nodes responsible for a more-specific prefix, or (2) an acknowledgment that a Map-Server will handle the request.

The rig tool displays the results of each query step, showing the matched EID-prefix, the type of response (node referral, map-server acknowledgement, or negative), the TTL, and the addresses of the next nodes to query. It also measures round-trip time for each message exchange.

When the 'follow-all-referrals' option is used, rig explores the entire DDT hierarchy below a starting node. Otherwise, it selects one referral at a time and traverses one branch of the tree until reaching a Map-Server.
sections.plainLanguage: Rig asks a LISP node 'where is this address?' and the node either answers 'ask this other node' or 'I have a map server for that'. Rig shows you each step and how fast the answer came back.

sections.title: Command Syntax and Options
sections.content:
The basic rig command syntax is:

rig [instance-id <iid>] <eid> to <ddt-node> [follow-all-referrals]

The parameters are: an optional instance ID for VPN contexts, the EID being looked up (which may be a hostname or IP address), the RLOC address of the starting DDT node to query, and an optional flag to follow all referral branches.

Different implementations have slightly different syntax. Cisco IOS uses the format above, while NX-OS allows both hostnames and addresses. The tool provides immediate feedback showing each step of the DDT traversal and the referral information from each node, allowing operators to verify that the mapping database is correctly configured and responding as expected.
sections.plainLanguage: You type 'rig' with an address to look up, which LISP server to start asking, and optionally tell it to ask all the servers it finds. It then shows you the answer from each server.

sections.title: Operational and Diagnostic Benefits
sections.content:
RIG provides several key diagnostic capabilities for LISP-DDT networks. It allows verification that the delegation hierarchy is correctly configured, showing which DDT nodes are authoritative for which EID-prefix ranges. It can detect configuration errors, missing nodes, and incorrect referral mappings.

By reporting round-trip times, rig helps identify slow or problematic DDT nodes. It can also reveal problems with the LISP infrastructure itself, such as missing Map-Servers or misconfigured delegations. For network troubleshooting, rig is similar to tools like 'dig' for DNS, providing a manual diagnostic interface into an automated mapping database system.

The tool is particularly useful when provisioning new LISP sites or modifying the DDT hierarchy, as operators can immediately verify that their changes are reflected correctly throughout the delegation tree.
sections.plainLanguage: Rig helps network operators check if the LISP phone book is set up correctly and working fast. It's like testing that a phone directory actually has everyone's number in the right place.
